COURT-APPOINTED CHILD CUSTODY EVALUATIONS — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Alex Doe · Jane Doe

DECLARATION -- SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet addresses California's statutory scheme governing court-appointed child custody evaluators and investigators under Family Code Chapter 6 (Custody Investigation and Report, commencing with Section 3110), in a contested custody or visitation matter concerning Alex Doe between Jane Doe and John Doe pending in Los Angeles County. It describes what a court-appointed evaluation is, who may serve as an evaluator and the training and licensing requirements that apply, how evaluation costs may be allocated between the parties, the confidentiality of the resulting report and the sanctions for its unwarranted disclosure, a domestic-violence-specific interview safeguard, the right to cross-examine the evaluator, and a separate, heightened evaluation protocol that applies when a serious allegation of child sexual abuse is at issue. This is distinct from this project's Mandatory Child Custody Mediation information sheet, which addresses Family Court Services mediation and recommending counseling under a different Family Code chapter, and from its Guardian Ad Litem and Minor's Counsel information sheets, which address representation of the child rather than the evaluator's own role.

"COURT-APPOINTED INVESTIGATOR" IS A DEFINED TERM COVERING THREE KINDS OF PERSONNEL
Family Code Chapter 6 uses the term "court-appointed investigator" as an umbrella label. Section 3110 defines it to mean a probation officer, a domestic relations investigator, or a court-appointed evaluator, in each case directed by the court to conduct an investigation under this chapter. Where a reference is made in this document, or in an order concerning Alex Doe, to a "court-appointed investigator," that phrase can refer to any of these three types of personnel, not only to a licensed mental-health evaluator.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "As used in this chapter, “court-appointed investigator” means a probation officer, domestic relations investigator, or court-appointed evaluator directed by the court to conduct an investigation pursuant to this chapter."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3110, Cal. Fam. Code § 3110 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3110.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes only Section 3110's definition. It does not independently verify how a specific superior court in California actually staffs custody investigations -- for example, whether a given county uses in-house probation or domestic relations investigators, contracts with private evaluators, or some combination -- which varies by county and is not addressed by the statute itself. No case law interpreting this definition was reviewed (see this document's overall CourtListener disclosure).

A COURT MAY APPOINT AN EVALUATOR IN A CONTESTED CASE, AND REPORTS MUST BE FILED AT LEAST 10 DAYS BEFORE THE HEARING
In a contested proceeding involving child custody or visitation, Family Code section 3111(a) authorizes -- but does not require -- the court to appoint a child custody evaluator to conduct an evaluation, where the court determines doing so is in the child's best interest. Any such evaluation must be conducted according to standards the Judicial Council adopts under Section 3117, and a court may consider an evaluation, investigation, or report only if it was conducted consistent with those standards (minor, nonsubstantive errors do not disqualify a report). If the court directs a written report, it must be filed with the court clerk and served on the parties or their attorneys, and on any separate counsel appointed for Alex Doe under Section 3150, at least 10 days before the custody hearing.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "In a contested proceeding involving child custody or visitation rights, the court may appoint a child custody evaluator to conduct a child custody evaluation in cases where the court determines it is in the best interest of the child. The child custody evaluation shall be conducted in accordance with the standards adopted by the Judicial Council pursuant to Section 3117, and all other standards adopted by the Judicial Council regarding child custody evaluations. If directed by the court, the court-appointed child custody evaluator shall file a written confidential report on the evaluation. At least 10 days before a hearing regarding custody of the child, the report shall be filed with the clerk of the court in which the custody hearing will be conducted and served on the parties or their attorneys, and any other counsel appointed for the child pursuant to Section 3150."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3111(a), Cal. Fam. Code § 3111(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3111.)
  Known gap: Section 3111(a) does not itself define "best interest of the child" for purposes of deciding whether to order an evaluation, and does not list the Judicial Council standards it cross-references (those are adopted separately under Section 3117 and in California Rules of Court, which this clause does not independently fetch or quote). The statute is permissive ("may appoint"), not mandatory, and nothing in this clause should be read as stating that a court is required to order, or will order, an evaluation in any particular case. No case law addressing when a trial court's decision to grant or deny a request for an evaluation is an abuse of discretion was reviewed (CourtListener quota was exhausted at research time -- see this document's overall disclosure).

SINCE 2005, AN EVALUATOR MUST GENERALLY HOLD ONE OF SIX SPECIFIED LICENSES OR CERTIFICATIONS
Family Code section 3110.5(c) limits who may serve as a child custody evaluator -- whether appointed under this chapter, under Evidence Code section 730, or under the discovery statute governing mental examinations -- to six categories of licensed or certified professionals: a physician who is a board-certified psychiatrist or has completed a psychiatric residency; a licensed psychologist; a licensed marriage and family therapist; a licensed clinical social worker; a licensed professional clinical counselor; or a court-connected evaluator certified by the court as meeting the Judicial Council's qualifications for court-connected evaluators. An evaluator proposed to assess Alex Doe's custody or visitation situation must fit one of these six categories, subject to the narrow unavailability exception addressed in this document's companion clause on that exception.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "a person may be a child custody evaluator under this chapter, Section 730 of the Evidence Code, or Chapter 15 (commencing with Section 2032.010) of Title 4 of Part 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure only if the person meets one of the following criteria:(1) The person is licensed as a physician under Chapter 5 (commencing with Section 2000) of Division 2 of the Business and Professions Code and either is a board certified psychiatrist or has completed a residency in psychiatry.(2) The person is licensed as a psychologist under Chapter 6.6 (commencing with Section 2900) of Division 2 of the Business and Professions Code.(3) The person is licensed as a marriage and family therapist under Chapter 13 (commencing with Section 4980) of Division 2 of the Business and Professions Code.(4) The person is licensed as a clinical social worker under Article 4 (commencing with Section 4996) of Chapter 14 of Division 2 of the Business and Professions Code.(5) The person is licensed as a professional clinical counselor under Chapter 16 (commencing with Section 4999.10) of Division 2 of the Business and Professions Code.(6) The person is a court-connected evaluator who has been certified by the court as meeting all of the qualifications for court-connected evaluators as specified by the Judicial Council pursuant to subdivision (b)."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3110.5(c), Cal. Fam. Code § 3110.5(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3110.5.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes only the six-category licensing list in subdivision (c). It does not restate the separate education, experience, and training requirements the Judicial Council was directed to formulate by rule under subdivision (b) (which this document does not independently fetch), and it does not verify the current text of California Rules of Court 5.220 or 5.225, which implement these qualification standards in more operational detail. This is a single statutory subdivision; no independent second source was located for it, and no case law addressing disqualification of an evaluator for failing to meet these categories was reviewed (CourtListener quota was exhausted at research time -- see this document's overall disclosure).

AN EVALUATOR MUST COMPLETE DOMESTIC-VIOLENCE AND CHILD-SEXUAL-ABUSE TRAINING AS A PRECONDITION TO SERVING
Independent of the licensing categories in Section 3110.5(c), Section 3110.5(a) requires that a court-connected or private child custody evaluator have completed the domestic violence and child abuse training program described in Family Code section 1816 and have complied with California Rules of Court 5.220 and 5.230 before serving in that role at all. Section 3110.5(f) adds a separate, later-enacted bar specific to child sexual abuse: on and after January 1, 2005, a court-connected or private evaluator may not evaluate, investigate, or mediate a custody issue unless that person has completed the child-sexual-abuse training the section requires.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "A person may be a court-connected or private child custody evaluator under this chapter only if the person has completed the domestic violence and child abuse training program described in Section 1816 and has complied with Rules 5.220 and 5.230 of the California Rules of Court."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3110.5(a), Cal. Fam. Code § 3110.5(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3110.5.)
  "On or after January 1, 2005, a court-connected or private child custody evaluator may not evaluate, investigate, or mediate an issue of child custody in a proceeding pursuant to this division unless that person has completed child sexual abuse training as required by this section."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3110.5(f), Cal. Fam. Code § 3110.5(f) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3110.5.)
  Known gap: This clause cites two different subsections of the same statutory section (§ 3110.5(a) and § 3110.5(f)); they are treated as one source, not independent corroboration. It does not independently fetch or quote Family Code section 1816 (the cross-referenced training-program statute) or Rules of Court 5.220/5.230, so the actual content and hour requirements of the training program are not verified here -- only the fact that completion is a statutory precondition to serving as an evaluator. No case law addressing the consequence of an evaluator's noncompliance with this training requirement (for example, whether it renders a report inadmissible or merely subjects the evaluator to licensing discipline) was reviewed (CourtListener quota was exhausted at research time).

THE COURT INQUIRES INTO ABILITY TO PAY BEFORE ORDERING REPAYMENT OF EVALUATION COSTS
When a court-appointed investigator is directed to conduct a custody investigation or evaluation, or to undertake related visitation work, Family Code section 3112(a) requires the court to inquire into the financial condition of the parent, guardian, or other person charged with supporting Alex Doe. If the court finds that person able to pay all or part of the expense of the investigation, report, and recommendation, it may order repayment to the court of an amount it determines proper; under subdivision (b), that repayment is made to the court itself, which keeps accounts of the expenses and repayments and deposits the collections as the Judicial Council directs.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Where a court-appointed investigator is directed by the court to conduct a custody investigation or evaluation pursuant to this chapter or to undertake visitation work, including necessary evaluation, supervision, and reporting, the court shall inquire into the financial condition of the parent, guardian, or other person charged with the support of the minor. If the court finds the parent, guardian, or other person able to pay all or part of the expense of the investigation, report, and recommendation, the court may make an order requiring the parent, guardian, or other person to repay the court the amount the court determines proper."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3112, Cal. Fam. Code § 3112 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3112.)
  Known gap: The statute does not set a fee schedule, a cap, or a formula for allocating cost between two parents -- it leaves the amount to the court's determination after the required ability-to-pay inquiry, and does not distinguish here between a court-connected evaluator's cost and a private evaluator's cost (private evaluators are frequently paid directly rather than through court repayment, a distinction this section's text does not itself address). This clause quotes both subdivisions of a single statutory section; no independent second source was located, and no case law on how courts apply the ability-to-pay inquiry in practice was reviewed (CourtListener quota was exhausted at research time).

THE EVALUATOR'S REPORT IS CONFIDENTIAL, STIPULATED-IN AS EVIDENCE, AND ITS UNWARRANTED DISCLOSURE CAN DRAW SANCTIONS
Family Code section 3111 places several controls on the report itself, separate from the confidentiality rule this project's Move-Away Custody information sheet addresses (Section 3025.5). Under subdivision (b), the report may not be made available except as subdivision (a) or Section 3025.5 provides, or as described in Welfare and Institutions Code section 204 or Probate Code section 1514.5. Under subdivision (c), the report may be received in evidence on stipulation of all interested parties and, once stipulated in, is competent evidence as to everything it contains. Under subdivision (d), if the court finds an unwarranted disclosure of the written confidential report, it may impose a monetary sanction -- sufficient to deter repetition, potentially including attorney's fees and costs -- against the disclosing party, unless the party acted with substantial justification or other circumstances make a sanction unjust, and the court may not impose a sanction that would create an unreasonable financial burden on the sanctioned party. Subdivision (f) defines "unwarranted": a disclosure is unwarranted only if it is done recklessly or maliciously and is not in Alex Doe's best interest.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The report shall not be made available other than as provided in subdivision (a) or Section 3025.5, or as described in Section 204 of the Welfare and Institutions Code or Section 1514.5 of the Probate Code."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3111(b), Cal. Fam. Code § 3111(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3111.)
  "The report may be received in evidence on stipulation of all interested parties and is competent evidence as to all matters contained in the report."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3111(c), Cal. Fam. Code § 3111(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3111.)
  "If the court determines that an unwarranted disclosure of a written confidential report has been made, the court may impose a monetary sanction against the disclosing party. The sanction shall be in an amount sufficient to deter repetition of the conduct, and may include reasonable attorney’s fees, costs incurred, or both, unless the court finds that the disclosing party acted with substantial justification or that other circumstances make the imposition of the sanction unjust."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3111(d), Cal. Fam. Code § 3111(d) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3111.)
  "For purposes of this section, a disclosure is unwarranted if it is done either recklessly or maliciously, and is not in the best interest of the child."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3111(f), Cal. Fam. Code § 3111(f) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3111.)
  Known gap: This clause cites four different subsections of the same statutory section (§ 3111(b), (c), (d), and (f)); they are treated as one source, not independent corroboration. It does not restate subdivision (a) (appointment and filing, covered in this document's companion clause) or subdivision (e) (the Judicial Council's confidentiality-notice form requirement), and it does not independently fetch or quote Welfare and Institutions Code section 204, Probate Code section 1514.5, or Family Code section 3025.5 -- each is only cross-referenced here as subdivision (b) names it. No case law construing "recklessly or maliciously" for purposes of the unwarranted-disclosure sanction was reviewed (CourtListener quota was exhausted at research time).

A HISTORY OF DOMESTIC VIOLENCE TRIGGERS A RIGHT TO MEET WITH THE INVESTIGATOR SEPARATELY
Family Code section 3113 provides a specific safeguard distinct from this project's other domestic-violence-related custody clauses: where there has been a history of domestic violence between Jane Doe and John Doe, or where a protective order as defined in Section 6218 is in effect, the party alleging domestic violence -- by written declaration under penalty of perjury -- or the party protected by the order can require that the parties meet with the court-appointed investigator separately and at separate times, rather than together.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Where there has been a history of domestic violence between the parties, or where a protective order as defined in Section 6218 is in effect, at the request of the party alleging domestic violence in a written declaration under penalty of perjury or at the request of a party who is protected by the order, the parties shall meet with the court-appointed investigator separately and at separate times."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3113, Cal. Fam. Code § 3113 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3113.)
  Known gap: This is a single statutory section; no independent second source was located for it. The statute does not specify a deadline or procedural mechanism for making the request (beyond a written declaration under penalty of perjury by the alleging party), and does not address whether it extends to other participants in the evaluation process, such as collateral witnesses. No case law addressing this section was reviewed (CourtListener quota was exhausted at research time -- see this document's overall disclosure).

A PARTY DOES NOT LOSE THE RIGHT TO CROSS-EXAMINE THE INVESTIGATOR BY SOMETHING SAID OR DONE BEFORE RECEIVING THE REPORT
Family Code section 3115 protects a party's ability to cross-examine the court-appointed investigator about the evaluation. A statement -- written or oral -- or a course of conduct is not treated as waiving that right unless the statement was made, or the conduct occurred, after the report was received by the party or the party's attorney. Something Jane Doe or John Doe said or did before receiving the report on Alex Doe's evaluation therefore cannot, by itself, be used to argue that person gave up the right to cross-examine the investigator about it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "A statement, whether written or oral, or conduct shall not be held to constitute a waiver by a party of the right to cross-examine the court-appointed investigator, unless the statement is made, or the conduct occurs, after the report has been received by a party or the party’s attorney."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3115, Cal. Fam. Code § 3115 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3115.)
  Known gap: The statute addresses only when a waiver is not found (before the report is received); it does not describe what statements or conduct after receipt of the report would actually constitute a waiver, and does not itself set the procedure or timeline for requesting cross-examination (that is addressed by the Judicial Council guidelines under the companion Section 3117, referenced but not independently fetched or quoted in this document). This is a single statutory section; no independent second source was located, and no case law construing this waiver rule was reviewed (CourtListener quota was exhausted at research time).

A SERIOUS CHILD-SEXUAL-ABUSE ALLEGATION TRIGGERS A SEPARATE, HEIGHTENED EVALUATION PROTOCOL
Family Code section 3118 imposes minimum requirements on top of the general evaluation rules described elsewhere in this document, once a court determines there is a "serious allegation of child sexual abuse" in a contested custody or visitation case where an evaluator has been appointed or a case referred for evaluation. The statute defines that term specifically: a serious allegation of child sexual abuse means an allegation of child sexual abuse, as defined in Penal Code section 11165.1, that is based in whole or in part on statements the child made to law enforcement, a child welfare services agency investigator, a mandated reporter, or other court-appointed personnel, or that is supported by substantial independent corroboration under Family Code section 3011(a)(2)(B). Once triggered, Section 3118(a)(3) requires that any evaluation or investigation conducted under this section be performed by an evaluator or investigator who meets the Section 3110.5 qualifications described in this document's companion clauses, and Section 3118(b)(6) requires a confidential written report filed with the court clerk and served on the parties or their attorneys at least 10 days before the hearing.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "For purposes of this section, a serious allegation of child sexual abuse means an allegation of child sexual abuse, as defined in Section 11165.1 of the Penal Code, that is based in whole or in part on statements made by the child to law enforcement, a child welfare services agency investigator, any person required by statute to report suspected child abuse, or any other court-appointed personnel, or that is supported by substantial independent corroboration as provided for in subparagraph (B) of paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) of Section 3011."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3118(a), Cal. Fam. Code § 3118(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3118.)
  "Any evaluation, investigation, or assessment conducted pursuant to this section shall be conducted by an evaluator or investigator who meets the qualifications set forth in Section 3110.5."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3118(a)(3), Cal. Fam. Code § 3118(a)(3) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3118.)
  "File a confidential written report with the clerk of the court in which the custody hearing will be conducted and which shall be served on the parties or their attorneys at least 10 days prior to the hearing."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3118(b)(6), Cal. Fam. Code § 3118(b)(6) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3118.)
  Known gap: Section 3118 is a long, multi-part section; this clause quotes only the definitional sentence, the cross-reference to Section 3110.5 qualifications, and the report-timing requirement. It does not restate the section's detailed list of required investigative steps (agency consultation, review of the child welfare file, criminal-background-check information, the multidisciplinary child interview team process, a forensic medical examination or a written explanation for not seeking one), the report's required contents, the emergency-order carve-out in subdivision (a)(1), the family-court-mediation information handling in subdivision (c), the temporary-visitation-limitation consideration in subdivision (f), or the juvenile-dependency-proceeding suspension and coordination rules in subdivisions (g) and (h) -- all of which this document does not independently verify or quote. No case law applying this section was reviewed (CourtListener quota was exhausted at research time -- see this document's overall disclosure).

HOW THIS CHAPTER RELATES TO OTHER CALIFORNIA CUSTODY PROCEDURES
A Chapter 6 court-appointed child custody evaluation, as described in this document, is a distinct procedure from several others this project separately documents or that California law separately provides. It is not the same as Family Court Services mediation or recommending counseling under Family Code Chapter 11 (commencing with Section 3160), addressed in this project's Mandatory Child Custody Mediation information sheet -- a case can go through mediation, an evaluation, both, or neither. It is not the same as the appointment of counsel to represent Alex Doe under Section 3150, addressed in this project's Minor's Counsel information sheet, although Family Code section 3114 (not independently verified or quoted in this document) allows a court-appointed investigator to recommend that the court appoint such counsel. An evaluation under this chapter can also be ordered under, or run alongside, an evaluation under Evidence Code section 730 or the civil discovery statute governing mental examinations (Code of Civil Procedure section 2032.010 et seq.) -- Section 3110.5's evaluator-qualification rules apply across all three routes, but this document does not independently verify Evidence Code section 730 or the Code of Civil Procedure provisions themselves. Nothing in this document requests, orders, or predicts whether a court will order an evaluation in any specific case involving Alex Doe.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT -- NOT A COURT ORDER OR DETERMINATION
I, Jane Doe, and I, John Doe, each acknowledge that I have reviewed this information sheet describing California's statutory scheme for court-appointed child custody evaluations and investigations in connection with the matter concerning Alex Doe pending in Los Angeles County.

Executed on January 1, 2026.

☐ _________________________ Jane Doe, signature

☐ _________________________ John Doe, signature

[This information sheet is prepared for use alongside an actual filing or proceeding in the appropriate California superior court. It does not itself appoint an evaluator, does not order or request an evaluation, does not determine which of the six Section 3110.5(c) qualification categories a specific evaluator satisfies, and does not allocate evaluation costs between Jane Doe and John Doe. Only the court, applying Family Code Chapter 6 and the Judicial Council standards and forms it references, determines whether an evaluation is ordered in a specific matter concerning Alex Doe and how it proceeds.]
